utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Ekkehard Withopf, with Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Muriel Cauvin, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and our legal assistant, Mr. Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present, Mr. Withopf and Mr. Mundis, the representatives of the Prosecution, as well as the Prosecution's new case manager. The Trial Chamber would also like to greet the Defence teams and the accused, as well as everyone else present in the courtroom, in particular the court reporter, whose work enables us to follow everything that is being said in realtime. The Trial Chamber has to rule on the admission into evidence of two documents. One is in English and the other document is -- one is in B/C/S and the other is in English. It's the translation that was written by Senad Dautovic on the 12th of October, 1993. The Defence produced this document in the course of its cross-examination, and the Prosecution has objected to admitting this document into evidence. The Trial Chamber would like to remind everyone that in principle the Trial Chamber doesn't admit into evidence a document that has been contested by the witness. In this particular case, the witness in question was not familiar with this document and pointed out that at the time that the document was drafted he was in detention. Nevertheless, in the interests of justice, one may admit a document into evidence, and in this case the Trial Chamber has noted that this document related to the grammar school, the Gimnazija, which has been mentioned both in the indictment and in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, this document has been signed by Mr. Senad Dautovic, whose name is also contained in the pre-trial brief. This document also relates to a body described as the civilian police, the MUP. And in addition, this document appears in the Prosecution's footnotes in its pre-trial brief. For these reasons, the document will be admitted into evidence and DH53, DH53/E for the English translation will be the exhibit numbers given to these documents. So the exhibit numbers are DH53 and DH53/E. That is our ruling. We are going to now continue and hear a new witness. I don't think that any protective measures have been requested as of yet. Could the usher go and call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear what I am saying? Can you hear the interpretation of what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As you have been called to appear here as a witness for the Prosecution, you have to make a solemn declaration, but it is also necessary for the Trial Chamber to be able to identify the witness. Could you tell us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Sulejman Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your date of birth and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born on the 6th of January, 1936 in Vares, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ajdancik [phoen] number 1 in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your current position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am currently the deputy cantonal prosecutor in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, over ten years ago, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 20th of May, 1993 until June 1997, I was the high public prosecutor for the territory of the Zenica-Doboj canton and the Central Bosnia canton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before a national or international court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you will now be testifying, it is necessary to first make the solemn declaration. Could you read out the text of the solemn declaration that the usher will show you in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Before a witness testifies, the Trial Chamber usually provides the witness with some information. Your profession might make this unnecessary. But as the proceedings are very special and differ from the continental proceedings, I would like to inform you that you will have to answer the questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right in this courtroom. We call this the examination-in-chief. After the Prosecution has concluded its examination-in-chief, you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Defence. That will be their cross-examination. In addition, the three Judges sitting before you may at any time ask you some questions in order to clarify some of your answers or if they feel it is necessary. So these proceedings are very different from the ones you are familiar with in your country, but there are certain aspects that are nevertheless similar. So you won't be thrown off balance or perturbed by such a procedure. To the extent that this is possible, try to provide full and precise answers to the questions put to you. Since the proceedings are oral, your answers will be contributing to the determination of truth, and this is why the witness's answers are so important. If you don't understand the sense of a question, ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. If you feel that there are any difficulties, inform the Trial Chamber of the difficulties you encounter and we will deal with the matter. In addition, I would like to remind you of two provisions contained in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence followed by this Tribunal. But I'll just remind you of this, given your position. The Rules provide that if false testimony is given, a witness could be prosecuted. In addition, there is a Rule that concerns answers given by a witness that might incriminate the witness. Depending on the nature of the question put to a witness, the witness might realise that information he might provide could be used against him. The Trial Chamber could force the witness to answer the question, even if the witness doesn't want to answer the question, but in such a case what is said can't be used against the witness in any subsequent prosecution. So I just wanted to outline the Rules that govern these proceedings. Without wasting any more time, I'll turn to the Prosecution. I think Mr. Mundis will be conducting the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And let me add my morning greetings to everyone in the courtroom as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, you've told us that at the beginning of the war you were the high public prosecutor for the Zenica-Doboj canton and the Central Bosnia canton. Can you tell the Trial Chamber when you graduated from law school and when you did your bar exams, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated in Sarajevo, but at the first year of law school in 1958-1960, I enrolled in Belgrade. I completed my first year in Belgrade, and then I moved to Sarajevo, and I graduated in Sarajevo in 1964. I then immediately went to serve in the JNA. This lasted for one year. Then I was an intern in the Zenica municipal court. After the internship, which lasted for two years, I carried on for about half a year, passed the bar exam, and was then immediately appointed as a judge of the municipal court in Zenica. And while performing those duties, I was mostly involved in criminal affairs. If I may -- should I continue or do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- before you continue, Witness, let me ask you: What types of cases were heard before the Zenica municipal court, in terms of the seriousness of those cases, particularly criminal cases, as you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period and even today, municipal courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were trials which dealt with offences carrying penalties of over [as interpreted] ten years. All such cases were tried in municipal courts. And if it was over ten years, if there was the death penalty, this was -- such cases were tried at the district court, which was later named the high court. And in 1997, the high court was named the cantonal court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps there's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there's just a slight error in the transcript. When the witness mentioned the penalties in the municipal courts, he said that there were penalties for up to ten years. And on page 7 of the transcript, line 9, it says "over ten years."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could we clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we've understood that the limit was ten years, but please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, in the English transcript of your testimony, it states that "At that period and even today municipal courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were trials which dealt with offences carrying penalties of over ten years." My question, in order to clarify, is: Do municipal courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina try cases with penalties of over ten years or do they prosecute cases involving penalties of up to ten years?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Only up to ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before I stopped you to discuss the jurisdiction of the municipal courts, you were about to continue. Was there anything you wanted to add about the period when you were initially a municipal judge, following law school?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary. If you think it is, ask me a question and I'll answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let's continue, then. How long did you remain a municipal court judge in Zenica? From what period of time until what period of time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked for about three years at the municipal court, and then I found employment in an insurance organisation, the name of which is Zoil Sarajevo, the Zenica branch. I worked there for two years, and then after that, on the 1st of July, 1975, I was appointed as the judge of the district court in Zenica, which was later called the high court, that is to say, the cantonal court. These are all high courts, but when the name was changed into the high court, I really don't remember. I worked until the 20th of May, 1993 in those two courts, the district court - that is to say, the high court - I worked there as a judge, involved in criminal affairs, involved in trials, and in the capacity of president of the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the date of 20 May 1993. On that date, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, as of that day, or up until that day? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From the 20th of May, 1993 onwards, what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 20th of May, 1993, the government of the Zenica district was also named the district for the Travnik area for the prosecutor, because I couldn't take an oath in Sarajevo, because at the time Sarajevo was completely blocked. So I was the acting judge. And in 1993, I took an oath, again in Zenica - not in Sarajevo - I can't remember before whom. But from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina there was a decision according to which I would be appointed as the high public prosecutor definitely and officially as of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain the high public prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I remained in that position from the 20th of March -- sorry, the 20th of May, 1993 until the 4th of June, 1997, when the cantons were formed and the high public prosecutor's office was called the cantonal public prosecutor's office. The positions were the same. The jurisdiction was the same. Only the name changed, given the formation of cantons at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we need a clarification here. We have carefully followed your words, and I would like to be absolutely sure that before the 20th of May, 1993 you were a judge, and after that, after the 20th of May, 1993, you were appointed prosecutor. Am I right? You know that there is a distinction between a judge and a prosecutor under the continental law. Before the 20th of May, you were a judge; and after the 20th of May, you were a prosecutor. Is that right? Can you please clarify. Can you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very difficult for me to say anything more precise. A judge is a judge. Up to that time, judges also conducted investigations. As of the 1st of August last year, the investigating judge lost that power and now it is the prosecutor that carries out investigations, submits evidence before the court. But before that date, I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that before the 20th of May, you were a judge. Was there a prosecutor while you were judge, before the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. At that time, there was a higher prosecutor, a higher prosecutor. I was a judge of the higher court in Zenica, and there was also a higher prosecutor's office, and the higher prosecutor had its deputies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on 20 May 1993, you were appointed prosecutor, so you replaced the prosecutor who was in that position up to then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We needed that clarification. It was very important to the Judges. Proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at the time you were appointed the high public prosecutor from 20 May 1993 onwards, what was the territorial jurisdiction that your position had responsibility for?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: From 20 May 1993 onwards, we mostly dealt with the following municipalities, those which are called Tesanj, Zavidovici - not Zepce, because it was under the control of the Croatian Defence Council - Zenica, Kakanj, followed by Gornji Vakuf - that is in the Central Bosnia canton - Gornji Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, but not Vitez because it was under the absolute control of the HVO authorities. During that period of time, while I was higher prosecutor, the municipalities of Olovo, Vares, and Visoko belonged to the current Sarajevo canton, but for the third time, I repeat, Sarajevo was encircled. The judiciary could not function in that area, so a decision had been made to put me in charge of those three municipalities. Actually, they were four municipalities: Visoko, Breza, Vares, and Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, which public prosecutor had responsibility for Maglaj municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the municipal prosecutor, but he was within the jurisdiction of the higher prosecutor, and the municipal prosecutor had jurisdiction over the area where the municipal court in Maglaj has jurisdiction and could prosecute crimes for which -- which carried penalties of up to ten years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask for clarification. With respect to Maglaj municipality, you said: "It was the municipal prosecutor but he was within the jurisdiction of the higher prosecutor." When you say "the higher prosecutor," which prosecutor or which prosecution office are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the higher public prosecutor in charge of the ZD canton, as it is now, and it was me at the time; and also the Central Bosnia canton, as it is now. At that time, they were called districts. And I was in charge of those two districts, in terms of control, advisory functions, and similar things, and there were other municipal prosecutors and I was in charge of all of these municipal prosecutors in my districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kapetanovic, for clarification, when you refer to "districts," what districts are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The Zenica and the Travnik districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've told us a little bit about the relationship between the district or high public prosecutor and the municipal prosecutors. Can you elaborate upon that, in terms of responsibilities and supervision between the district prosecutor and the municipal prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, it was the office of the higher public prosecutor; although, that is not important. This person was in charge of crimes carrying a penalty of up to ten years in prison. Criminal reports -- and I'm talking about the civilian sector, it was only in 1992 when military prosecutors' offices would be set up. So the public prosecutor was independent in his work, but when it came to grave criminal acts, aggravated criminal acts, where he was in doubt whether he was indeed in charge and could be authorised, because it was likely that there might be a penalty of over ten years, then after consultations such a case would be referred to a higher public prosecutor in Zenica who would either accept that case, or the public prosecutor would meet with his deputies and conclude that they would continue hearing this case because this case would probably carry a penalty under ten years. Then they would proceed investigating that case. So this would be more or less the purview of the public prosecutor. Also, in such cases where a municipal prosecutor was facing a dilemma whether there was a criminal act involved that was prosecuted ex officio, then this municipal prosecutor would come for consultations to the higher public prosecutor, who would give him oral instructions in most cases, but sometimes he would also give him written instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I need some clarification from you, sir. We would like to be absolutely positive that when you were appointed, you were a prosecutor -- general prosecutor. You had under you other prosecutors to whom you gave either oral or written instructions. Can you please confirm that, that as of the 20th of May, 1993 you were the highest public prosecutor in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that there is no doubt about that. As far as the district is concerned, later on the canton, the position of a prosecutor, a higher public prosecutor at the time - and now the cantonal prosecutor - is the highest possible position, in terms of a state body. At that time, a state body in charge of prosecuting persons that may have committed crimes. As of the 1st of August last year, prosecutors also carry out investigations, present evidence before Trial Chambers during the main hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, Witness, at the time in 1993, from May 20th, 1993 onwards, as the high public prosecutor for Zenica and Travnik, you had supervisory responsibility over approximately 12 municipal prosecutors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to sum up, the municipal prosecutors could prosecute cases carrying penalties up to ten years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And any cases carrying penalties of greater than ten years would automatically be handled by the high public prosecutor, rather than the municipal prosecutors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, from -- or during the period from 20 May 1993 through 1994, what body of criminal law and criminal procedure was being applied by the courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Once the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised, the Presidency started passing decrees with legal effect. Pursuant to these decrees, a lot of the codes and laws that were in force in the former Yugoslavia were adopted. There was also a decree, but I can't tell you when it was published in the Official Gazette, by which the Criminal Code of the former Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted, as well as the criminal procedure code, and we continued implementing and applying those laws in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. our everyday practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So to clarify, Witness, in 1993 and 1994 the courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina were applying the Criminal Code and criminal procedural code of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of international crimes were set forth in the Criminal Code of the SFRY that was applied by courts in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the regulations, Chapter 16, I believe it was, we were in charge of the crimes of genocide and war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the international law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the penalties for violation of the crimes of genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the international law?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Such crimes carried a minimum of five years in prison, I believe. I'm not sure. But I don't think it's important, because you can find it in the law. Genocide was a minimum of 10 years or 15 years. There was also a death penalty. The death penalty was abolished either in 1997 or in 1998, if my memory serves me right. The death penalty could have been substituted by a prison sentence of 20 years, especially if there were mitigating circumstances, the death penalty could have been substituted either during the first instance procedure or during the second instance procedure. It could be substituted by a higher instance court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, from the period when you were appointed high public prosecutor on 20 May 1993 through 1994, which courts within the districts that you were responsible for had jurisdiction over these crimes set forth in Chapter 16 of the Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The courts responsible for such crimes were the higher prosecutor and the higher court. There was a higher court and there was also a newly established military court. When the military court was established - I believe that it was in late 1992 - it had jurisdiction over all the crimes carrying penalties under ten years and over ten years. But military courts were also in charge of military personnel, all the military structures, officers, cadets, reserve officers, members of the MUP, the police, that is, if they were involved in war operations. Military courts were also in charge of the civilians who may have committed a crime targeting military facilities or objects of military importance. In this specific case, I believe that it is important for me to say that the military court in charge of crimes against humanity and the international law was also in charge of civilians, if those civilians committed a crime together with a military person. They were also in charge of civilians if some other crimes were committed jointly by a civilian and by a military person. On the other hand, the civilian courts were only in charge of civilians. Truth be told, there were a lot of dilemmas as to whether a person was a civilian or a soldier. There was a state of chaos, and there were numerous cases in which a civilian would steal or borrow clothes or weapons. He would still be a civilian; however, he would be wearing a uniform, and in this uniform he would commit a grave crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you a few questions, in terms of clarification from your answer. But first, let me return to the issue of the civilian municipal courts. Did those courts, the civilian municipal courts, in the area that you were responsible for, prosecute crimes or cases under Chapter 16 of the Criminal Code during the period 1993-1994?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't be responsible for prosecuting this type of crimes. I don't know of a single case in which a municipal court would prosecute such a case. I suppose -- I hope it won't sound impertinent if I say that this would not have made any sense at the time, to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. You've told us about a state of chaos, and there were numerous cases in which a civilian would steal or borrow clothes or weapons. What steps were taken to ensure that alleged perpetrators were prosecuted in the correct court, in terms of the civilian court or the military court? What steps were taken?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: In such cases, I believe that there was an absolute cooperation between the military and the civilian courts, and the prosecutor's office as well, needless to say. It largely depended on the type of crime. If we're talking about robberies, aggravated robberies, murders - and there were a lot of such cases - and possibly rapes, as far as I remember all the steps were taken in order to bring the perpetrator to justice. During the relevant period of time, I believe that we have quite a number of such cases. We're talking about civilians who either stole, borrowed, or get hold -- got hold of both a uniform and weapons in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've mentioned there was absolute cooperation between the civilian and military courts. What -- again, what type of steps did you take, or did this cooperation take to determine whether an alleged perpetrator was a civilian or a member of the military?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. There was an absolute cooperation between the civilian and the military police, and needless to say there was also cooperation between the civilian and military prosecutor's office and the civilian and military courts. And if you'll allow me, it was very often dubious whether a person was a soldier or not. At the beginning, records were not kept, so when we started prosecuting a certain case, we had to establish the truth based on what the perpetrator himself told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us a few moments ago about the establishment of district military courts. And I'll ask you more detail about that in a moment. But among the persons that you told us those courts had jurisdiction over were members of the MUP and the police. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you know, why a military court would have jurisdiction over the MUP and the police.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I said that. If I did, I'd like to deny that. I'm talking only about cooperation. The times were chaotic, and all I'm saying is that the military police and the civilian police cooperated -- the civilian police, that is. Then if you will allow me, we would then try to establish whether the person had to be tried by the civilian court or the military court, based on what I have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps my question wasn't clear, Witness. A few moments ago you told us whom -- over whom the district military courts could exercise jurisdiction. Do you remember who could be brought before a district military court?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than members of the army, who else could be brought before district military courts?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Civilians too, if they had perpetrated a crime together with soldiers. And this involved our cooperation. This is when we would have to assess the type of crime committed. We had to assess whether something had been perpetrated against armed forces, whether the soldier was the main perpetrator. So it all depended on the particular case. There was not just one set of rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to return to this issue because in the English transcript at page 16, lines 7 through 10 - and I just want to make sure the transcript is correct - you said: "The military court had jurisdiction all the military structures, officers, cadets, reserve officers, members of the MUP, the police, that is, if they were involved in war operations."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This is transcript page 16, lines 7 through 10. So the military courts did have jurisdiction over members of the MUP and the police when involved in war operations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Witness. At the time you were appointed the high public prosecutor on 20 May 1993, did you have a staff of other prosecutors to assist you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did. May I tell you how many? May I provide you with their names? Would you like the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, please, if you can tell us how many and the names of those prosecutors who worked in your office, that is, the high public prosecutor's office from 20 May 1993 through 1994.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 20th of May, 1993 up to 1994 - that's how the question was put - as I have already mentioned, I was the prosecutor. There was Halilagic Suada, who is now the state court prosecutor; there was Curic Semsa, who has now retired, as well as myself, given our age. There was Dzemaludin Mutapcic, who at the time was the deputy of the republican prosecutor. And as he couldn't go to Sarajevo because of the blockade, he was sent to work with me. And this was a very diligent person, I have to say that, whose work amounted to the work of two deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe for the Court the conditions under which your court operated or the -- the court that you appeared before operated from 20 May 1993 through 1994?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, with regard to this period, the high prosecutor's office and the court functioned, but the conditions were very difficult. We didn't have paper. We didn't have ink. Often there was no electricity, there was no food. Either there wasn't enough food or there wasn't any at all. We were under blockade, and I wasn't able to coordinate with the territory of the Travnik canton, not on a daily basis at least. So it was difficult to work, but the work was done somehow. And I think that this could be proved and supported by information from that period, information about the number of criminal cases, about the number of trials, judgements, naturally, the type of crimes perpetrated. All this can be established with official information, and it would be far more reliable than my answers to your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber how your office obtained information, how investigations were carried out, et cetera, how your office functioned from the beginning of, perhaps, a police complaint through the process. Can you briefly describe that for the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, and while those laws were in force, we dealt with cases on the basis of criminal charges filed by the civilian police, that is to say, the centre -- the security services centre, which covered a number of municipalities and what is now the Zenica and Doboj canton. So I'd like to repeat that this was done on the basis of criminal charges filed by the civilian police. And if in the meantime the perpetrator of the crime was identified by the military police and if he was identified as a civilian, then naturally this case was sent to us. If you ask me about the particular case in question, I couldn't tell you anything, because a lot of time has passed since then. And all this information can be reliably confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, again, my question wasn't clear, Witness. I'm simply asking for a brief explanation of how the process worked once your office received a police report from the centre for security. What happened? How was an investigation carried out? How was the procedure? How was an indictment drafted? If you can briefly just tell the Trial Chamber how that functioned in the period 20 May 1993 through 1994.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the procedure. When we received a criminal report, we would examine it. If it didn't contain sufficient information, we would ask the police to check up on certain information. If the criminal report was complete, then we'd make a request for an investigation, to the extent that this fell within our remit. We would submit a request for an investigation to the investigating judge of the cantonal court in Zenica. He would carry out the investigation on the basis of our request. But if he saw that the request that we had submitted was valid and complete, he would then decide on carrying out an investigation. And according to the criminal -- the law on criminal procedure in force at the time, the criminal procedure would be instigated. The investigating judge would instigate this procedure on the condition that everything was in order, provided that the accused could be heard and provided that access could be gained to the accused, as well as to witnesses and expert witnesses. Again, it depended on the type of criminal case in question. And once all this had been done, on the basis of the request for carrying out an investigation, and on the basis of the instructions from the prosecution, then the case would be referred to the cantonal court and the deputy of the public prosecutor would be responsible for it -- I'm sorry, of the high public prosecutor. That's the period we are talking about. An indictment would be then issued, or if no crime had been committed, the proceedings would be suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kapetanovic. From the period 20 May 1993 through 1994, what type of involvement did you as the high public prosecutor have in issues relating to war crimes or crimes against humanity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it would be superfluous to say the following in the light of your question: My main concern was to gather information on genocide and war crimes. To this very day, I have worked hard on this. As soon as I was appointed, three or four days later I contacted all the bodies that might be involved in this area and that should be involved in this area, the area of genocide and war crimes. I contacted them with regard to gathering information. On that occasion - and I even have everything noted down in my notebook, which I haven't consulted since then - I summoned the representatives of the civilian police. I also summoned the military prosecutor, who was present. And at the time, there was a centre for investigating war crimes. There was a state commission for gathering information -- for gathering evidence on war crimes. I believe there were about 20 people to whom I assigned tasks as of that date, because you could only gather information. You couldn't institute proceedings. So this was done in Bugojno and in Zavidovici and even in Doboj. And my colleagues from Tuzla, from Mostar, and from Bihac came to see how I carried out this work on one occasion, because gathering statements in centres, in police stations or at the state commission, where I happened to be the president, such statements aren't that reliable and legally valid, but I always insisted on this being forwarded to the investigating judge, who should take statements according to the regulations. And quite a lot of work was done in this way. If that is your question, I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask -- let me ask you this, Witness: In the period again from May 20th, 1993 through 1994, from whom were you gathering this information with respect to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, I exclusively received information from the security services centre. And naturally, in cooperation with them and the prosecutor, et cetera. Because this was quite new, as far as crimes were concerned, so we were trying to find our bearings, and that is perhaps still the case today. But on the whole, we received criminal reports from the civilian police, reports which we were able to process in the standard way. And if there was evidence, a request would be submitted to the investigating judge, who would conduct an investigation. After having conducted the investigation, he would refer the matter to the prosecutor and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, I'm speaking specifically about investigations with respect to war crimes from 20 May 1993 through 1994. You've told us that you received information from the security services centre. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's absolutely correct. It couldn't be otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall who the victims that were being interviewed about these war crimes from 20 May 1993 through 1994? Who was the security service interviewing, in terms of the victims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: There was ethnic cleansing. I remember people expelled from Kozarac who arrived in the territory of the Zenica. That was in 1992. And likewise, from the area of Bratunac a large number of refugees arrived and I insisted on them being interviewed so that they could provide us with the relevant information. And then naturally, we insisted on having the investigating judge interview those witnesses. Again, I would like to repeat that only such statements were reliable. And another thing: During the conflict between the BH army and the HVO - and this is something I found out later - Bosniak refugees arrived in the territory of Zenica. Again, the investigating judge would take statements from them; although, the commissions I have mentioned also got involved in this to a certain extent. And at the time of these conflicts - and that was in the middle of 1993, as far as I can remember, perhaps in April or May - Croats either withdrew or went to Vitez, where they took refuge. This is where the HVO was in power. And colleagues would then take statements from Croats and gathered evidence in this manner, whereas, we gathered our evidence from Bosniaks. In the meantime, after the cantons had been formed, in 1996 we exchanged this evidence and the indictments. We sent them to these people, to the court that had jurisdiction in Travnik, and in return they would send us other cases. So with regard to gathering evidence, this is how we did it during the conflict. This was the only way to do it. To do it in any other way would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me return to several things that you said in response to my last question. You talked about people being expelled by Kozarac. The people -- what was the ethnicity of the people expelled from Kozarac and what was the ethnicity of the perpetrators that you were investigating with respect to those refugees from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the conflict between the BH army and the HVO, I as a civilian prosecutor didn't have -- didn't know anything about this. What I said a minute ago is something that I found out about later, after we had exchanged information on the cases. And I realised that Croat colleagues in Vitez had taken statements from them, just as they'd taken statements from refugees. At the time, I wasn't in a position to know whether they were refugees or not or whether they had left of their own accord. Given the fact that there was a conflict, it would be absurd to think that the civilian public prosecutor had any information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, perhaps my question wasn't clear. Let me ask you. You mentioned refugees from Kozarac, and I'd like to focus your attention on the refugees from Kozarac. What was the ethnicity of the refugees from Kozarac and what was the ethnicity of the alleged perpetrators who may have committed crimes against the people who arrived from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Your question was well phrased a minute ago. I didn't answer it, but I did answer it partially. As far as the refugees are concerned, I found out later on in 1996, on the basis of information from colleagues who had gathered information in Vitez from the district military court. But as to the perpetrators, I was not able to know anything about this. If there were any such perpetrators, I can't know anything about this. Only the military prosecutor or the military police could have knowledge about this matter. But as far as the information I had as a prosecutor, I had none. When a war is raging, the situation is terrible. Naturally, a civilian isn't in contact with anyone, and as a result has no information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the period from 1993 or May of 1993 through 1994, how many cases did the high public prosecutor's office in Zenica, that is, your office, investigate where it was alleged crimes were committed by soldiers of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as war crimes are concerned, in particular with regard to Bosniaks, I can only remember one case in that period of time. Zahiragic [phoen] Dzemal was the name of the person concerned. And if you will allow me to say this -- yes, this happened later on. It was a matter dealt with my the military court. Zahiragic, as a member of the Serbian army, when he was in Batkovici he looted Bosniak property in the territory of Bijeljina and other villages for the benefit of his superiors. He would enter houses, get hold of property that was mobile, and surrender it to his superiors. And I also remember that he would take jewellery from detainees and everything else they had on them. And he even maltreated them mercilessly. He would beat them. One of the civilians detainees from that camp was so severely beaten by him that he succumbed to his injuries. Again, as far as I can remember, that case was dealt with in 1993 by the judge in the district military court in Zenica. I even think that he was given the death penalty. As to what subsequently happened in that case, I think that the case was -- was suspended -- I think it was transferred to the civilian court. I have just remembered - but I'm not absolutely sure, but perhaps there is information about this too - from October 1994, as the international community had insisted on this, crimes against humanity or international law were supposed to be dealt with by civilian courts. When dealing with crimes of this nature, the military courts were supposed to be excluded. When this decree law was adopted, the particular case that you have asked me about was referred to a civilian court, which then rendered an appeals judgement. That is one case I could mention. When I was interviewed in September of last year, I remembered four cases quite by chance, the one I have mentioned and another three cases, and I know for sure that this was something that happened in 1993 again. In the middle of 1993, the military court tried Vinko Vidovic, if I'm not mistaken, who together with a number of HVO members entered the village of Loncari in Busovaca municipality. He was armed, and started perpetrating ethnic cleansing. I don't know how many civilians he took prisoner. I know it was an odd number, four, five, or nine -- five, seven, or nine. And he shot those people and he took some of them to a prison that had been formed by the HVO in Busovaca. And I remember that this criminal case was dealt with by the district military court in Zenica as far as the following two cases are concerned. I can remember someone called Dusko Pasalic from the area of Vozuca in the Zavidovici municipality and he committed a crime in an identical manner, but in the year 1992, in the same way that Vinko Vidovic had committed a crime. They shot about ten Bosniaks. Among other things, we established that he had personally killed one Bosniak. So with regard to Dusko Pasalic, they were involved in ethnic cleansing. They expelled inhabitants from the village and then looted their property. And this criminal case was dealt with by a civilian court. It would appear at a later date because as I have said, the decrees I have mentioned were in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. force -- although, he was a member of the Serbian army. Can I continue, or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, Witness, we were at the time when we normally take a short break for technical reasons. So perhaps you can tell us about the fourth case after the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now have a break and resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, shortly before we broke, you were about to tell us about the fourth case involving war crimes that you recalled being prosecuted in 1993 or 1994. Can you tell us about that fourth case, if -- if you remember anything about it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you what I remember. I remember the name, Vinko Kajic. This is the name that came up very often. This person was a member of the HVO. And together with a number of other members of the HVO, they were armed and they stormed into a village. There may have even been more than one village involved. I'm not sure. This was in the territory of Gornji Vakuf or Prozor municipality. We collected evidence from the statements from the victims, mostly women, older women and younger women alike. He stormed into the village. The villagers -- the male villagers were not in the village, or so it seems. They were either on the front line or somewhere else. He ordered those women and girls to line up. He took gold and jewellery from them. He provoked them. He insulted them. He was very brutal to them. Maybe it's not the place for me to say and describe all those bestialities. Together with other members of the HVO, he took some young women away. I don't know whether they raped them or not. I can't remember at the moment. He either raped them or attempted to rape them. In any case, I've had hundreds of cases of women and young girls who were raped, but they were reluctant to speak about that in court. They were ashamed. So this may have been the case as well. This crime was prosecuted by a civilian court; although, he was a member of the HVO. This crime was probably only heard after the decree was passed for all the cases that were supposed to be seen by military courts to be referred to the civilian courts. And this is all I can say about this particular case, about this particular crime. Two crimes were prosecuted by the military court and two crimes were prosecuted by the civilian court during the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, do you recall in the case involving Vinko Kajic that you just described for us what the ethnicity of the victims in that case was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Bosniaks, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, of the four cases that you've just told us about, did any of those cases involve alleged perpetrators of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina against Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not have any such cases. Had I had them, they would have been prosecuted. In any case, I believe you can consult the official records and find information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, during the period from 20 May 1993 through 1994, how much involvement, if any, did you have with military leaders in the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not clear on the question. Are you referring to my contacts with them? Is that the gist of your question? Are you referring to my possible contacts with these people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with any possible contacts. From 20 May 1993 through 1994, did you have any contacts with the military leaders of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I had contacts -- official contacts with the military prosecutor once I was appointed. As far as the officers are concerned, I did not have any contact with them whatsoever, nor was this contact required. They had other things and problems on their mind, so they did not have time to contact me in my capacity as a civilian prosecutor. They were in a very difficult position. There was no arms, no clothes. They had their own problems pertaining to their purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, from 20 May 1993 through 1994, how much contact, if any, did you have with the military police of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember having had any contact, but the civilian police cooperated with the military police in cases of aggravated crimes which were committed jointly by civilians and by the troops. This was up to the moment when the military prosecutor was in charge of prosecuting such cases. I remember that they did cooperate; I didn't, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, from 20 May 1993 through 1994, how much contact, if any, did you have with the military security service of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this very well. It was in mid-June 1993 when I learnt that from the area of Susanj, Ovnak, Janjac or that general area 17 corpses were brought to the pathology of the cantonal hospital in Zenica and civilians. There were rumours about it, and I believe that Vlado Adamovic told me about that. Vlado Adamovic was in charge of identifying those bodies. I remember - and I will never be able to forget - that some 10 or 15 days later, at the proposal of my deputy, Suada Halilagic, who had arranged a meeting, we went to see Ramiz Dugalic, the chief of security of the 3rd Corps. He received us. We had a conversation with him. When we learnt that civilians may have been involved in that, I must admit that I was surprised because the army was absolutely loyal to the late President Izetbegovic and he was the one who kept on saying, "Don't touch the property or the civilians of other ethnic groups. Don't touch their religious facilities." And that's why I was surprised, and that was also the reason why I went to see Mr. Dugalic. We had this conversation. On that occasion, he told us that he was aware of the fact that the civilians had been victims of war operations. They got involved in the conflict involving the BiH army. I was curious to find out whether the civilians may have been involved in this crime. He convinced me that they weren't, and this is how our conversation ended. Later on I found out that some other bodies were brought at a later date, but I wasn't interested, in my professional capacity, and he assured me that if anything like that had happened, that only the military prosecutor would have jurisdiction over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, do you recall what area or town or village these 17 corpses were recovered from that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I can repeat. It was Susanj, Ovnak, Janjac and some other villages in that area in the territory where the HVO had already dug out their trenches. I don't know who against. I know that there were trenches in the area. I don't know where the barrels were facing. In any case, it was on the border between Zenica and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These 17 corpses, do you know the ethnicity of these people that were killed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats to the last. According to the official documents, they were all Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they were civilians or members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence objects to these questions because this incident is not part of the indictment. This incident is not covered in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber turns toward the Prosecution. You've heard the objection by the Defence. The Defence says that the incident involving Croatian civilians and troops are not part of the indictment. Can the Prosecution explain the reasons for putting these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would submit that this line of questioning, which is virtually complete, goes to the issue of notice to the accused. As the witness has testified, Ramiz Dugalic was the chief of the security section of the 3rd Corps of the ABiH. One would -- the Prosecution will be able to demonstrate throughout this trial that that would be an issue that should have been reported -- that this issue involving these 17 people should have been reported up the chain of command to the accused, and it simply puts him on notice of crimes committed within his area of responsibility, which the Prosecution would submit would be part of the notice that the accused received that these types of crimes were being committed, and should have either been prevented or punished thereafter. So it goes, Mr. President, to the issue of notice to the accused, with respect to criminal acts being committed within his area of responsibility and of which his security chief was aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The Prosecution has explained why this question was put. According to the Prosecution, it goes to the issue of notice to the accused that such crimes were committed. Mrs. Residovic, you want the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to object to the comment by my learned friend from the Prosecution. The witness has not spoken about crimes. The witness has spoken about the corpses, the 17 bodies which were brought to the mortuary of the hospital. This witness has not provided any grounds based on which the Prosecutor might conclude on any crimes having been committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber makes note of your observation, and that is that the witness has never spoken about any crime. Is the Prosecution finished with the prosecution -- with the examination-in-chief, or are there any other questions to be put to the witness by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are a couple of additional lines of questions that the Prosecution would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, during the period from 20 May 1993 through 1994, how many cases, if any, were referred to your office by the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember a single one. There may have been such cases. I would like to refer you to the official records, because frankly speaking I don't remember. I don't remember. If you had given me a task to check, I would have done it and I would be able to testify about that as I sit here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, earlier this morning, before the break, you told us about the district military courts. Do you recall in the Zenica or Travnik areas when the district military courts were established?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: It was in autumn 1992, possibly in September. Most probably in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did the district military courts exist or when did they stop functioning?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: When they were established, there were two military district courts, in Zenica and in Travnik. They operated up until the 30th of June, 1996, when this decree came into effect. The handover was carried out on the 1st of August, 1996. There are official records on the handover listing all the crimes, their numbers, their perpetrators, all the crimes that were handed over by the military courts to the competent civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where do you know -- do you know where the records from the Zenica and Travnik military district courts are located today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: All these records are in the cantonal prosecutor's office in Zenica or in the cantonal court in Zenica, depending on the stage of the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've described for us earlier this morning how, on the civilian side, there were both municipal courts and district courts. Did that same structure apply to the district military courts? In other words, were there lower-level military courts at the municipal level or were there only the district military courts in Travnik and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I've already answered that. I can only repeat. District military courts were in charge of all the crimes carrying penalties under ten years and over ten years, and the appeals were heard by the civilian state court. I would just like to add to that that Sarajevo was under blockade. We established a department of the supreme court in Zenica, and this was the appellate court which heard the appeals referred to it both by the civilian district court and the military district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period from May 20th, 1993 through 1994, do you recall who was the military prosecutor for the Zenica district military court?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Mula-Arifovic Kemal was in that position. He is currently retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the same period, that is, from May 20th, 1993 through 1994, do you recall who was the military prosecutor for the Travnik district military court?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Behaja Krnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier you told us -- or you mentioned the name Vlado Adamovic. During the period 20th May 1993 through 1994, can you tell the Trial Chamber who Vlado Adamovic is and what position he had in that period.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado Adamovic was a judge of the district military court in Zenica. I know for a fact that he tried a lot of cases in his capacity as a military judge. Currently Vlado Adamovic is a judge of the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if you will allow me to say that another judge was Mladen Veseljak. The two of them were in charge of the military district courts and presidents of trial chambers. They served both as first-instance-court judges and appeals judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than Vlado Adamovic, do you recall the names of any of the other judges at the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember Hidajet Halilagic. I remember Hilmo Ahmetovic. I remember only the first names of the two, who were refugees; one was Hasan and the other was Atif or Arif.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the name Mladen Veseljak. Which district military court was he a judge of?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a judge of the military district court in Zenica, and later he was a judge of the cantonal court, until a month or two months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of the judges at the Travnik district military court?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember any. I remember just one deputy; his name was Meho Bradaric. When this military prosecutor's office was disbanded, then the staff joined the civilian prosecutor's office, both from Travnik and from Zenica. And that is why as of the 1st of August, 1996, I had as many as 16 deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, during the period 20 May 1993 through 1994, do you recall if your office had any involvement with cases that ultimately ended up being prosecuted before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic, I remember. We even drafted an indictment. We collected evidence. But at that time -- and I don't know how it happened that you accepted that, because it was even before the Rome Accord, which was passed on the 16th of February, 1996. We collected ample evidence for Dario Kordic. We submitted a request for an investigation to be carried out. And you probably know much better than I do, although I am a witness here, how this case was referred here. There was just a request for an investigation, and an investigating judge of the cantonal court in Zenica issued a decision on carrying an investigation, and this was again referred to the ICTY. And these are the two cases from the area that I remember very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Defence takes the floor, I have a number of legal questions I would like to ask you in order to clarify some of your answers, some of which appear quite vague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we don't have the criminal procedural code from ex-Yugoslavia, as you are a legal person, your answers can certainly provide us with additional information. In your capacity as prosecutor, who was above you? Who was your superior? Was there a Minister of Justice? Was there some body above you, or was there no such body? What could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, there was the republican prosecutor, who was my superior. But we were not actually able to establish contact. I have on numerous occasions already said that it was the account of the total blockade of Sarajevo. We could only communicate via fax. And there was a republican prosecutor who was above me as well. And if you have no objection to me saying the following, I'd like to say that the deputy of the republican prosecutor, Dzemaludin Mutapcic, had been sent to work. So I was able to contact someone from the republican prosecutor's office in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have taken note of the fact that your superior was in Sarajevo but that because of the circumstances you were unable to communicate with him. I'd also like to know something else. You mentioned this a while ago but it wasn't quite clear. When there was a complaint or when there were facts that could be -- or events that could be described as criminal, according to what you have said, the civilian police conducted an investigation. This -- a report of the investigation was forwarded to you in order to institute prosecutions. But in your capacity, could you yourself conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: The security services centre, that is to say, the police, carried out the investigation, checked up on the information, and filed a criminal report. The investigation at the request of the prosecution was carried out by the investigative judge from the court, but they were involved in the investigation. But there was a law, 145, paragraph 2 of the ZKP, the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was in force at the time. According to this law, if the prosecutor heard about the perpetration of a crime, it was his responsibility to take the necessary measures. And because of those provisions, I tried to carry out certain verifications. So if I had any information, then I asked in writing that the security services centre, that is, the police, check up on this matter. And after they had done that, regardless of whether it was a criminal report or some sort of report, the Prosecution had the right to -- and the possibility to conduct an investigation, as it had certain evidence that had been gathered about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you have provided a very precise legal answer to this question. When Mr. Dugalic tells you that as far as he knows the civilian or military victims -- well, apparently you didn't have any jurisdiction. You didn't have the right to check up on what this person had said. Were you satisfied with what he had said? In your capacity, were you not supposed to check up on this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the decree law, I went to see Mr. Dugalic to verify whether civilians had participated in the affair. He said that he was aware of the fact that they were victims but that they were the victims of an armed conflict. He persuaded me that this was the case. But believe me, I didn't believe that the army could do something like that, if the army actually did it. I was surprised. How could the army do such a thing? I satisfied myself with that answer, and -- well, in any event, civilians couldn't have participated in the armed conflict, so that couldn't have fallen within my remit. When the military court was in function, it was on the 10th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this information. In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution, you mentioned a commission that had been established. Its responsibility was to carry out investigations into war crimes. This is what you yourself said. Who were the members of this commission? You were a member, but who were the other members?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: That was the state commission for gathering evidence on war crimes. I was its president. Someone important from Sarajevo insisted on me being the president, because they had heard that I was successful in dealing with this. The others were colleagues, lawyers, who hadn't passed the bar exam but they were only working in the field and tried to check up on where the injured parties were located, and they would provide me with information. They were investigators of a kind. They tried to determine who the relevant witnesses might be. We then forwarded the information to the prosecution or to the court so that reliable statements could be taken from these persons. Naturally, at the time it was not -- you couldn't conceive of me being both the prosecutor and the president of the state commission, but the situation was such. So I allowed this to happen and I had people, apart from the civilian police, who went into the field to determine the location of various persons and to take brief statements from them. And we would then forward these statements to the investigating judge of the cantonal court in Zenica, for them to be further examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As a prosecutor, did you have any competence with regard to matters of personal liberty. If someone had been detained or captured, did you have any competence as far as personal liberty is concerned? Your procedural code, did this code allow you to play a role in that matter or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember anything of that kind happening. It was never necessary for me to intervene. If anything happened and when it happened, this was following a suggestion from the Prosecution. The investigating Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. judge should decide on carrying out an investigation and on the detention. But I don't remember anything of this kind. Whether something of this nature existed in the military prosecutor's office, that is to say, the military court, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question, which concerns legal affairs: At the end of the examination-in-chief, you said that the military courts, when appeals were filed, you said that the civilian courts were competent if there was an appeal. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in agreement with the president of the supreme court of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we decided to form a department in Zenica which would deal with appeals from the civilian high court and the military court. There was no higher body that would cover the military or high court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have clarified these legal issues, which might have appeared a little vague. But you have provided us with all the necessary information. I'll now turn to the Defence, who will commence their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Kapetanovic. My name is Edina Residovic. I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic. Mr. Kapetanovic, we know each other from before the war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, General Hadzihasanovic's Defence, in the course of its investigation, in the archives of the military court obtained a certain number of documents, so I will be asking Mr. Kapetanovic if he could also tell us something about these matters. I wanted to inform the Trial Chamber of this, as I will be using a number of these documents in the course of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kapetanovic, in response to a question from my learned colleague from the Prosecution, you said you were a judge in the municipal court in Zenica and then you were a judge in the Zenica high court up until the 20th of May, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 20th of May, 1993 - and I am only repeating what you yourself have said - you were appointed as the prosecutor of the high public prosecutor's office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was named as the acting high public prosecutor, as I couldn't take an oath, given the fact that Sarajevo was under a complete blockade. So I only took an oath on the 5th of October of the same year. I have already said that, and I am repeating it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it also be correct to say - and I think that this is something you have said already - that as a judge of the municipal court and then as a judge of the high court, and in particular in your capacity as a prosecutor, you were involved in criminal affairs exclusively; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, and that is absolutely correct. And I worked on these affairs as the president of the chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When holding these positions, you performed your duties in accordance with the law which was in force at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For these reasons and also because of the fact that the Prosecution asked you many questions that had to do with the application of law and the functioning of the judicial system, allow me to ask you some questions that relate to this sphere. Would it be correct to say that the high public prosecutor's office in Zenica before the war covered the territory of the high court in Zenica and at the time it covered 12 municipalities, Zenica, Zavidovici, Bugojno, Busovaca, Donji Vakuf, Gornji Vakuf, Kakanj, Kupres, Novi Travnik, Travnik, Vitez, and Zepce? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in the course of the war, there were occasional changes in the territorial jurisdiction of the high court and the high public prosecutor's office because of the situation that was as a result of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, some of the municipalities that were under the jurisdiction of the high public office -- high prosecutor's office were under the control of the Serbian forces, so it wasn't possible to carry out the legal functions of the high public prosecutor's office and the high court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition, at the end of 1992, and in particular in 1993, the so-called Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna issued decisions on establishing special courts and prosecutor's offices that were to be active in the area of Herceg-Bosna; that is to say, in the area under the control of the Croatian Defence Council. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN KAPETANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And in particular, in Vitez, Zepce, Busovaca, and I can't remember the other places.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
